content: {"id": "c9805a1f-9a15-40e6-8313-e0f36a4314cf", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "186007ab-2516-4cc2-9837-6ffc53248278", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "Application Load Balancer versus Network Load Balancer"}]}

{"id": "071f2399-dd91-4024-9328-36ea90818328", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Both are AWS Elastic Load Balancing options, but they work at different layers and suit different use cases:

**Application Load Balancer (ALB)**
- Operates at Layer 7 (application layer, HTTP/HTTPS)
- Routes traffic based on content — URL path, hostname, headers, query strings
- Supports advanced routing: path-based, host-based rules, redirects, fixed responses
- Native support for containers via target groups (great fit for ECS/EKS)
- Supports WebSockets, HTTP/2, gRPC
- Handles SSL/TLS termination with rich cert management
- Best for: web applications, microservices, APIs where you need smart routing decisions

**Network Load Balancer (NLB)**
- Operates at Layer 4 (transport layer, TCP/UDP/TLS)
- Routes based on IP protocol data — extremely high throughput, low latency
- Can handle millions of requests per second with minimal latency overhead
- Supports static IP addresses per Availability Zone (and Elastic IPs) — useful when clients need to allowlist fixed IPs
- Preserves the source IP of the client by default
- Best for: latency-sensitive apps, TCP/UDP traffic, gaming, IoT, or when you need a static IP endpoint

**Quick rule of thumb:** if you're routing HTTP/HTTPS traffic and need content-aware decisions, go with ALB. If you need raw performance, static IPs, or non-HTTP protocols, go with NLB.
